lesson.title: Why Atoms Stick Together: An Overview of Chemical Bonding
lesson.summary: This section previews the major categories of chemical bonds and interactions, from strong ionic and covalent bonds to weaker hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces, and explains the shared underlying principle: atoms bond to reach a more stable, lower energy arrangement of electrons.
lesson.body:
A chemical bond is an attractive force that holds atoms together, and nearly every important structure and process in biology, from the shape of a protein to the double helix of DNA to the membrane surrounding every cell, ultimately depends on the specific bonds atoms form with one another. Bonds exist because atoms are more stable, meaning lower in potential energy, when their outermost electron shell is full. Most of the atoms discussed in the previous section, carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur, do not have a full outer shell on their own, so they gain stability by sharing, donating, or attracting electrons in ways that fill that shell, whether through a bond with one other atom or through a network of many weaker interactions.

Chemical bonds and interactions in biology fall into a few broad categories that differ mainly in how the electrons involved are shared and how much energy is required to break them. Ionic bonds form when one atom transfers an electron or electrons to another atom entirely, creating two oppositely charged ions that attract each other electrostatically. Covalent bonds form when two atoms share a pair of electrons between them rather than transferring them outright, and covalent bonds are generally the strongest bonds found in biological molecules, which is why they form the backbone of large molecules like proteins, carbohydrates, and nucleic acids. Hydrogen bonds are a weaker, different kind of interaction that forms not between whole atoms sharing or trading electrons, but between a hydrogen atom already covalently bonded to an electronegative atom and a second electronegative atom nearby, and they are individually weak but collectively powerful when many of them act together. Van der Waals forces are weaker still, arising from brief, shifting imbalances in electron distribution rather than any fixed charge, yet they still matter enormously at the molecular scale.

A useful way to organize these categories is by relative strength and the physical basis of the attraction: ionic and covalent bonds both involve major rearrangements of electrons between or around atoms and require substantial energy to break, while hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces involve much smaller charge imbalances and break and reform constantly at biological temperatures. This is not a weakness of the weaker bonds so much as a different design purpose. Strong covalent bonds are ideal for building the fixed, load bearing skeleton of a molecule, the sugar phosphate backbone of DNA for instance, while weak, reversible hydrogen bonds are ideal for connections that need to come apart and reform easily, such as the base pairing between the two strands of the DNA double helix, which must separate temporarily every time a cell copies its genetic material or reads a gene.

The remainder of this chapter examines each of these bond types in turn: ionic bonds and covalent bonds first, since they involve the most dramatic electron rearrangements, then hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces, which depend on the polar covalent bonds discussed along the way, and finally water polarity and cohesion and adhesion, which show how these bonding principles combine to give water the unusual properties that make life as we know it possible.
